t.en: In this section, we will use elementary matrices to prove a useful theorem about the inverse of a square matrix. We start with an observation about the echelon form of a right invertible matrix.

title.en: Echelon form of a right invertible matrix

t.en: Suppose that $A$ is right invertible. Then the reduced echelon form of $A$ does not have a row of zeros.
Let $R$ be the reduced echelon form of $A$. Then by Theorem “The form $R=UA$”, we can write $R=UA$ for some invertible square matrix $U$. By assumption, we have $AB=I$, and therefore
If $R$ had a row of zeros, then so would the product $R(BU^{-1})$. But since the identity matrix $I$ does not have a row of zeros, neither does $R$.

title.en: Right invertible square matrices are invertible

t.en: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are square matrices such that $AB=I$. Then it follows that $BA=I$, and therefore $B=A^{-1}$. In particular, a square matrix is right invertible if and only if it is left invertible if and only if it is invertible.

Assume $A$ and $B$ are square matrices such that $AB=I$. Let $R$ be the reduced echelon form of $A$. Then by Theorem “The form $R=UA$”, we can write $R=UA$ where $U$ is an invertible matrix. Since $AB=I$, we know by Lemma “Echelon form of a right invertible matrix” that $R$ does not have a row of zeros. Since $R$ is a square reduced echelon form with no row of zeros, each column must be a pivot column, and it follows that $R=I$. Hence, $UA=I$, and therefore $A$ is left invertible. Moreover, we have
and therefore $B=U$. It follows that $BA=UA=I$, as claimed.

To prove the last claim, note that we just proved that for square matrices, $AB=I$ implies $BA=I$. Therefore, every right inverse of $A$ is also a left inverse, and therefore an inverse. But of course, we also have that $BA=I$ implies $AB=I$. This is just the same theorem, with the roles of $A$ and $B$ interchanged. Therefore, every left inverse of $A$ is also a right inverse.

This theorem is very useful, because it allows us to test only one of the products $AB$ or $BA$ in order to check that $B$ is the inverse of $A$, saving us half of the work. It is important to stress, however, that this only works for *square* matrices. As we saw in Example “Right inverse”, non-square matrices can be right invertible without being left invertible, or vice versa.
